source_text: ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ΙΑʹ. Περὶ φθόνου. Ἀγαθὸς ὁ Θεὸς, καὶ ἀγαθῶν τοῖς ἀξίοις παρεκτικός· πονηρὸς ὁ διάβολος, καὶ κακίας παντοίας δημιουργός. Καὶ ὥσπερ ἕπεται τῷ ἀγαθῷ ἡ ἀφθονία, οὕτως ἀκολουθεῖ τῷ διαβόλῳ ἡ βασκανία. Φυλαξώ μεθα οὖν, ἀδελφοὶ, τὸ πάθος τοῦ φθόνου, μὴ κοινω νοὶ τῶν ἔργων τοῦ ἀντικειμένου γενώμεθα, καὶ εὑρε θῶμεν τῷ αὐτῷ συγκαταδικαζόμενοι κρίματι. Εἰ γὰρ ὁ τυφωθεὶς εἰς κρῖμα ἐμπίπτει τοῦ διαβόλου, πῶς ὁ φθονερὸς τὴν ἡτοιμασμένην τῷ διαβόλῳ τι μωρίαν ἐκφεύξεται; Φθόνου γὰρ πάθος οὐδὲν ὀλεθριώτερον ψυχαῖς ἀνθρώπων ἐμφύεται· ὃς, ἐλάχιστα λυπῶν τοὺς ἔξωθεν, πρῶτον κακὸν καὶ οἰκεῖόν ἐστι τῷ κεκτημένῳ. Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἰὸς σί δηρον, οὕτως ὁ φθόνος τὴν ἔχουσαν αὐτὸν ψυχὴν ἐξ αναλίσκει. Μᾶλλον δὲ ὥσπερ τὰς ἐχίδνας φασὶ τὴν κυήσασαν αὐτὰς γαστέρα διεσθιούσας ἀπογεννᾶσθαι, οὕτω καὶ ὁ φθόνος τὴν ὠδίνουσαν αὐτὸν ψυχὴν πέφυκε δαπανᾷν. Λύπη γάρ ἐστι τῆς τοῦ πλησίον εὐπραγίας ὁ φθόνος. Διόπερ οὐδέποτε ἀνίαι, οὐδέποτε δυσθυμίαι τὸν βάσκανον ἐπιλείπουσιν. Εὐφόρη σεν ἡ χώρα τοῦ πλησίον; εὐθηνεῖται πᾶσι τοῖς κατὰ τὸν βίον ὁ οἶκος; θυμηδίαι τὸν ἄνδρα οὐκ ἐπιλείπουσι; ταῦτα πάντα τροφὴ τῆς νόσου, καὶ προσθήκη τῆς ἀλγηδόνος ἐστὶ τῷ βασκάνῳ. Ὥστε οὐδὲν διαφέρει ἀνθρώπου γυμνοῦ παρὰ πάντων τιτρωσκομένου. Ἀνδρεῖος τίς ἐστιν; εὐεκτεῖ; ταῦτα πλήττει τὸν βάσκανον. Ἕτερος χαριέστερος τὴν μορφήν; ἄλλη πληγὴ τῷ βασκάνῳ. Ὁ δεῖνα τοῖς τῆς ψυχῆς προτερήμασι τῶν πολλῶν ὑπερέχει; ἐπὶ φρονήσει καὶ δυνάμει λόγων ἀποβλέπεται καὶ ζηλοῦται; ἄλλος πλουτεῖ καὶ φιλοτιμεῖται λαμπρῶς ἐν ἐπιδόσεσι καὶ κοινωνίᾳ τῇ πρὸς τοὺς ἐνδεεῖς, καὶ πολὺς αὐτῷ παρὰ τῶν εὐεργετουμένων ὁ ἔπαινος; ταῦτα πάντα πληγαὶ καὶ τραύματα, μέσην αὐτοῦ τύπτοντα τὴν καρδίαν. Καὶ τὸ χαλεπὸν τῆς νόσου, ὅτι οὐδὲ ἐξειπεῖν αὐτὴν δύναται· ἀλλὰ κύπτει μὲν, καὶ κατηφής ἐστι, καὶ συγκέχυται, καὶ ποτνιᾶται, καὶ ἀπόλωλεν ὑπὸ τοῦ κακοῦ. Ἐρωτώμενος δὲ τὸ πάθος, ἐρυθριᾷ δημοσιεῦσαι τὴν συμφορὰν, ὅτι Βάσκανός εἰμι καὶ πικρὸς, καὶ ἐπιτρίβει με τὰ τοῦ φίλου καλὰ, καὶ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ τὴν εὐθυμίαν ὀδύρομαι, καὶ οὐ φέρω τὴν θέαν τῶν ἀλλοτρίων καλῶν, ἀλλὰ συμφορὰν ποιοῦμαι τὴν τῶν πλησίον εὐημερίαν. Ταῦτα γὰρ ἂν εἴποι, εἰ τὰ ἀληθῆ λέγειν βούλοιτο. Ὧν οὐδὲν ἐξειπεῖν αἱρούμενος, ἐν τῷ βάθει κατέχει τὴν νόσον ὑποσμύχουσαν αὐτοῦ τὰ σπλάγχνα καὶ κατεσθίου σαν. Οὐκοῦν οὔτε ἰατρὸν τῆς νόσου παραλαμβάνει, οὔτε τι φάρμακον ἐξευρεῖν δύναται τοῦ πάθους ἀλεξητήριον, καίτοι πλήρεις αἱ Γραφαὶ τῶν ἰαμάτων τούτων· ἀλλὰ μίαν ἀναμένει τοῦ κακοῦ ῥᾳστώνην, εἴ πού τινα ἴδοι καταπεσόντα τῶν φθονουμένων. Οὗτος ὅρος τοῦ μίσους, ἄθλιον ἰδεῖν ἐκ μακαρίου τὸν βασκαινόμενον, ἐλεεινὸν γενέσθαι τὸν ζηλωτόν. Τότε σπένδεται, καὶ φίλος ἐστὶν, ὅταν δακρύοντα ἴδῃ, ὅταν πενθοῦντα θεάσηται. Καὶ εὐθυμοῦντι μὲν οὐ συνευφραίνεται· ὀδυρομένῳ δὲ συνδακρύει. Καὶ τὴν μεταβολὴν τοῦ βίου, ἐξ οἵων εἰς οἷα μεταπέπτωκε, κατοικτίζεται, οὐχ ὑπὸ φιλανθρωπίας, καὶ τοῦ συμ παθὴς εἶναι, ἐξαίρων τῷ λόγῳ τὰ πρότερα, ἀλλ' ἵνα βαρυτέραν αὐτῷ κατασκευάσῃ τὴν συμφοράν. Τὸ παιδίον μετὰ τὸν θάνατον ἐπαινεῖ, καὶ μυρίοις ἐγκωμίοις ἀποσεμνύνει, ὡς μὲν καλὸν ἰδεῖν, ὡς δὲ εὐμαθὲς, ὡς δὲ πρὸς πάντα εὐάρμοστον· οὐκ ἂν αὐτῷ περιόντι γλῶσσαν εὔφημον χαρισάμενος.
orientation: Basil opens his homily by contrasting God's generosity with the devil's malice, then describes how envy torments the envious person from within.
pass_a_gloss: Homily 11. On envy. God is good, and a provider of good things to the worthy; the devil is wicked, and a craftsman of every kind of evil. And just as freedom from envy follows the good one, so envy follows the devil. Let us guard ourselves, then, brothers, from the passion of envy, lest we become sharers in the works of the opponent, and be found condemned together with him in the same judgment. For if the one puffed up falls into the judgment of the devil, how will the envious person escape the punishment prepared for the devil? For no passion more destructive than envy grows in the souls of human beings; which, grieving least those outside, is a first evil and one's own to the one who possesses it. For just as rust consumes iron, so envy consumes the soul that has it. But rather, just as they say vipers are born by eating through the belly that conceived them, so also envy by nature devours the soul that gives birth to it. For envy is grief at the prosperity of the neighbor. Therefore never do pains, never do depressions leave the envious person. Did the neighbor's land bear well? Does the house thrive in all the things of life? Do joys not leave the man? All these things are food of the disease, and an addition of the pain to the envious person. So that he differs in nothing from a naked man wounded by all. Is someone brave? Is he in good condition? These things strike the envious person. Is another more graceful in form? Another blow to the envious person. Does so-and-so surpass the many in the advantages of the soul? Is he looked upon and envied for wisdom and power of words? Does another grow rich and seek honor splendidly in gifts and in fellowship toward the needy, and is there much praise for him from those who are benefited? All these things are blows and wounds, striking the middle of his heart. And the difficulty of the disease is that he is not even able to speak it out; but he bows down, and is downcast, and is confounded, and laments, and is destroyed by the evil. And when asked about the passion, he blushes to make public the misfortune, that 'I am an envious person and bitter, and the good things of my friend wear me down, and I lament my brother's cheerfulness, and I do not bear the sight of others' good things, but I make the prosperity of my neighbors a misfortune.' For these things he would say, if he wished to speak the truth. Choosing to speak out none of these things, he holds the disease down in the depth, smoldering and eating his inward parts. Therefore he neither takes a physician for the disease, nor is able to find any remedy as a defense against the passion, although the Scriptures are full of these healings; but he awaits one relief from the evil, if he should ever see one of those envied fallen. This is the limit of the hatred: to see the envied one wretched from blessed, the envied one to become pitiable. Then he makes a truce, and is a friend, when he sees him weeping, when he beholds him mourning. And with one rejoicing he does not rejoice together; but with one lamenting he weeps together. And he pities the change of life, from what things into what things he has fallen, not out of love for humanity, and not from being sympathetic, exalting in speech the former things, but in order that he may make the misfortune heavier for him. The child after death he praises, and magnifies with countless encomia, as beautiful to see, as quick to learn, as well-suited to everything; though he would not have granted him a well-speaking tongue while he was alive.

choices.why: The participle means 'the one set against'; Basil uses it as a title for the devil, distinct from διάβολος, so I keep the literal sense rather than collapsing it into 'the devil'.
The alpha-privative noun is the opposite of φθόνος; rendering it as 'freedom from envy' preserves the wordplay with the homily's subject.
The verb τυφόω means to be deluded or puffed up with pride; 'puffed up' keeps the physical image Basil uses for the proud person's fall.

choices.english: the soul that gives birth to it
choices.why: The verb ὠδίνω means to be in birth pangs; Basil's image is of envy being born from the soul and then devouring it, so 'gives birth to' preserves the metaphor.
rejected: the soul in travail with it

choices.why: The verb means to burn slowly underneath; 'smoldering' captures the hidden, consuming fire of envy inside the person.
The adjective means 'able to ward off'; rendering it as 'defense against' keeps the military sense of protection from the passion.

pass_b_english: God is good, and He gives good things to those who deserve them. The devil is evil, and he is the craftsman of every kind of wickedness. And just as abundance follows the good, so envy follows the devil. Let us guard ourselves, then, brothers, from the passion of envy, so that we do not become partners in the works of the opponent and find ourselves condemned under the same judgment as he is. For if the one who is puffed up falls into the judgment of the devil, how will the envious person escape the punishment prepared for the devil?

No passion grows in human souls more destructive than envy. It causes the least grief to those outside, but first and chiefly it is an evil belonging to the one who harbors it. Just as rust consumes iron, so envy consumes the soul that holds it. Or rather, just as they say vipers are born by eating through the womb that conceived them, so envy by its nature consumes the soul that is in labor with it. For envy is grief at a neighbor's prosperity. That is why grief and despondency never leave the envious person alone.

Has his neighbor's field produced a rich harvest? Does his household overflow with all the goods of life? Does joy never leave the man? All these things are food for the disease and an increase of pain for the envious person. So he is no different from a naked man being wounded by everyone. Is someone brave? Is he in good health? These things strike the envious person. Is another more graceful in appearance? That is another wound for the envious person. Does so-and-so surpass the many in the advantages of the soul? Is he admired and envied for his wisdom and power of speech? Does another grow rich and win honor splendidly through his gifts and his sharing with the needy, and does he receive great praise from those he has helped? All these things are blows and wounds, striking the envious person in the very middle of his heart.

And the harsh thing about the disease is that he cannot even speak of it. He hangs his head, and he is downcast, and he is troubled, and he laments, and he is undone by the evil. But when he is asked about his suffering, he blushes to make public his misfortune, that "I am envious and bitter, and the good things of my friend wear me down, and I grieve over my brother's cheerfulness, and I cannot bear the sight of another person's good things, but I make my neighbor's prosperity into my own misfortune." These are the things he would say if he wanted to speak the truth. But since he chooses to say none of them, he keeps the disease deep within, smoldering and consuming his inward parts.

So he neither calls in a doctor for the disease, nor can he find any medicine as a defense against the passion, even though the Scriptures are full of these remedies. Instead he waits for one relief from the evil: if he should somehow see one of those he envies fall. This is the limit of his hatred: to see the envied person become wretched instead of blessed, to see the one envied become pitiable. Then he makes peace, and he is a friend, when he sees him weeping, when he watches him mourning. He does not rejoice with him when he is cheerful, but he weeps with him when he laments. And he pities the change in his life, the fall from what he had to what he has now—not out of love for humanity or because he is compassionate, but so that by extolling in words his former state he can make his misfortune heavier. He praises the child after its death and honors it with countless eulogies—how beautiful to look at, how quick to learn, how well suited to everything—though he would never have given it a kind word while it was alive.

ἀφθονία means abundance/generosity, not 'freedom from envy'
problems.ruling: ἀφθονία means 'abundance/generosity,' not 'freedom from envy'; contrast with βασκανία (envy) is lost

fixed: τὸν ζηλωτόν means 'the one envied,' not 'the one he admired'; changed to 'the one envied'.
ἀφθονία means abundance/generosity, not 'freedom from envy'; changed to 'abundance'.

problems.quote: but it is first and foremost an evil that belongs to the one who possesses it
problems.source_quote: πρῶτον κακὸν καὶ οἰκεῖόν ἐστι τῷ κεκτημένῳ
problems.why: πρῶτον means 'first' temporally or 'in the first place' (i.e., primarily), not 'first and foremost' in a superlative sense; the point is the evil begins at home.
problems.fix: but first and chiefly it is an evil belonging to the one who harbors it

problems.quote: by praising his former state in words he can make his misfortune heavier
problems.why: ἐξαίρων means 'taking away/removing,' not 'praising'; he removes former goods in speech to worsen the contrast.
problems.fix: by taking away his former state in words he can make his misfortune heavier
problems.ruling: ἐξαίρων is middle voice of ἐξαιρέω ('take away/remove'), not ἐπαινέω ('praise'); 'removing' former goods in speech creates contrast to worsen misfortune.

problems.quote: so envy by its nature devours the soul that gives birth to it

problems.why: ὠδίνουσαν means 'in labor/travail with it,' not 'gives birth to it'; the soul is pregnant with envy, not its mother in a generative sense.
problems.fix: so envy by its nature consumes the soul that is in labor with it
problems.ruling: ὠδίνουσαν means 'in labor/travail,' not 'gives birth'; soul travails with envy, not birthing it.
